title: With most information hidden, the game Stratego had stumped AI—until now
gist: Academic researchers from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, NYU and Stanford built Ataraxos, which beat Stratego great Pim Niemeijer 15-1 with four draws, after training on just 16 GPUs for a week (a few thousand dollars) versus an estimated $3M-$4.5M for DeepMind's weaker DeepNash. Key innovations were a belief model enabling search under hidden information, a GPU simulator, and annealed self-play updates; the team pitches applications to war gaming, negotiations and markets.

insights.claim: DeepNash was trained for two to three months on 1,024 Google chips, an estimated $3 million to $4.5 million at 2025 prices, while Ataraxos needed 16 GPUs for a week plus four GPUs for four days for its belief model, costing a few thousand dollars.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Algorithmic and simulator efficiency can deliver ~1000x cost reductions, undercutting the thesis that frontier results require massive compute.
insights.quote: a run the Ataraxos team estimates would cost $3 million to $4.5 million at 2025 prices

insights.claim: Ataraxos played about 34 times fewer training games than DeepNash yet ended up much stronger, aided by a GPU simulator running millions of moves per second.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: GPU-native simulation is a key lever for cheap RL, relevant to agent-training economics.
insights.quote: it played about 34 times fewer games than DeepNash, and still ended up much stronger.
insights.locator: The algorithm also learned far faster

insights.claim: A team from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, New York University and Stanford succeeded at Stratego where DeepMind, despite its exceptional budget, could not reliably beat top humans.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Academic labs can still leapfrog big-tech labs in specialized AI domains, limiting compute moats.
insights.quote: Even DeepMind, with its exceptional budget, couldn’t build a machine that reliably beat the best human players.
insights.locator: Deep Blue took down Garry Kasparov

insights.claim: Stratego is hard for AI because it has over a decillion possible setups and games that can last 2,000 moves, versus 1,326 hidden-hand combinations in Texas Hold'em and about 40 moves in chess.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Long-horizon, high-hidden-information settings resemble real strategic domains and were a frontier of AI capability.
insights.quote: In chess, usually the game lasts 40 moves, but in Stratego, a game can easily last 2,000 moves,
insights.locator: In chess, usually the game lasts

insights.claim: Ataraxos's key innovation was a second neural network, a belief model, that guesses the opponent's hidden pieces from their movements so the AI can sample plausible arrangements and search ahead, which DeepMind could not make work.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Belief-model sampling makes test-time search tractable in imperfect-information settings, a transferable technique for agents.
insights.quote: The solution was a second neural network, a belief model, trained to guess the opponent’s hidden pieces based on how they had been moving.
insights.locator: This is one of the things

insights.claim: Ataraxos learned through 163 million self-play games, using big strategy updates early and small careful ones later to stop hidden information from sending learning in circles.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Simple training schedule changes can unlock stability in hard RL problems.

insights.claim: Ataraxos beat Pim Niemeijer, a four-time world champion with over 600 weeks ranked number one, 15 games to one with four draws over three weeks of online play.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Another major strategy game falls to AI, reinforcing capability momentum in imperfect-information reasoning.
insights.quote: beat Pim Niemeijer, arguably the best Stratego player of all time, 15 games to one, with four draws

insights.claim: At the 2025 Stratego World Championship, Ataraxos won 38 of 40 games against challengers and shifted the metagame, for example by often hiding its flag in a corner behind just two bombs.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: AI strategies are reshaping human expert practice, a pattern likely to repeat in professional domains.
insights.quote: I think this bot has kind of skewed the metagame a little bit,

insights.claim: Because machines can ignore secrets they know when acting, Ataraxos leaves weak spots alone if the opponent has no reason to suspect them and calmly 'bluffs' back from as low as a two percent win probability.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: AI's emotionless deception in adversarial settings has implications for negotiation and trading agents.
insights.quote: We would watch the bot ‘bluff’ its way back from like a two percent victory probability, very, very casually,

insights.claim: The same Ataraxos approach beat three world champions at Barrage Stratego, mastered the cooperative card game Hanabi, and beat the best bots at dou dizhu.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A general imperfect-information method, not a one-game trick, increases applicability.

insights.claim: The researchers argue the gap between board games and real problems like negotiations, financial markets and military conflicts is smaller than it looks, and their techniques can be used for war gaming against strong opponents.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Cheap strategic-reasoning AI could find defense and trading applications, with dual-use implications.
insights.quote: You can use the techniques that were derived here to play it forward and see how a strong opponent might respond to what you do.
insights.locator: War gaming is a common thing

insights.claim: Ataraxos cannot explain its moves, and the team says interpretable, explainable strategies are not yet achieved.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Lack of explainability limits adoption in regulated, high-stakes real-world settings.
insights.quote: I think we’re not quite there yet,
